decisions.quote: The central finding of the present analysis is that overeducated workers have worse career prospects than correctly allocated workers. This is in clear contrast to the results put forward by Sicherman (1991). Note, however, that we were able to replicate the US results with our German data when using Sicherman’s approach. Therefore, the key to understanding the puzzling pattern of results is to be found in a discussion of the validity of the indicators chosen to indicate upward career mobility, and the quality of specification in Sicherman’s model.
decisions.location: Section 5 (Conclusions), p. 18, lines 954-966 (also Section 4.1, pp. 10-12, lines 588-683; Section 4.2, p. 15, lines 820-826)
decisions.reason: In Section 4.1 (Table 2, Columns II-III), the authors closely replicate Sicherman's (1991) occupational upward-mobility specification using German GSOEP data and obtain the same positive, statistically significant effect for overeducation. However, their central argument is that Sicherman's specification and indicator are flawed: controlling for starting occupational rank ('base'/ceiling effects, Table 2, Column V) renders the overeducation effect insignificant, and replacing occupational rank moves with a valid indicator of upward career mobility (relative wage growth controlling for base wages, Section 4.2, Tables 3-4) reverses the effect. Under the codebook rules, obtaining the original effect with the original approach while demonstrating as the paper's main message that the original method/specification does not validly test the hypothesis is coded as 'statistically successful but flawed'. The shipped coding ('failed') relied only on the abstract's summary of the wage-growth specification.

corrected_value.title: Career mobility, job match, and overeducation

decisions.quote: In Section 4.3, we extend Robst’s (1995) test for robustness by using an objective, as well as a subjective, measure of training participation. Both measures confirm Robst’s findings that overeducated (undereducated) workers indeed receive less (more) training than correctly allocated ones.
decisions.location: Section 1 (Introduction), p. 3, lines 190-198; Section 4.3, pp. 16-17, lines 864-920
decisions.reason: Omitted target in shipped data. Beyond citing Robst (1995) as background, the paper explicitly re-tests Robst's (1995) empirical finding on training participation in Section 4.3 (Tables 5 and 6) using the same subjective survey question in the German GSOEP sample as well as an objective formal training indicator, concluding that both measures confirm Robst's findings.
